title: Hyderabad Water Stress Index
description: Composite water-stress index across 186 Hyderabad sections, built by merging five civic datasets: tanker deliveries, connections, billing, groundwater and water bodies.
introText: Which parts of Hyderabad are most at risk of water shortages, and is the problem getting worse? This project combines several open datasets into one section-level view of the city, scores each area's water stress, maps the results, and forecasts tanker demand.
methodology:
Five datasets (water tankers, connections, billing, groundwater, and water bodies) were merged to cover 185 Hyderabad water-supply sections from January 2022 to February 2024. Most of the effort went into cleaning:
- Section names were standardized across datasets, and sub-zones were merged into their parent sections.
- Non-residential entries such as reservoirs, treatment plants, and control rooms were removed.
- About 29 corrupted billing values were nulled out rather than guessed.
- Sections were geocoded, and failed lookups were fixed manually.
- Each section was matched to its nearest groundwater station and to the water bodies within 3 km.

A composite water stress score was then built from five indicators: tanker dependency, groundwater depletion, billing gap, unmet connection demand, and water body scarcity. The scoring went through three iterations (min-max, z-score, then clipped z-score) before the map gave a sensible picture. The result was validated with Moran's I and LISA spatial analysis, 121 years of rainfall data were tested for a trend, and a trend-plus-seasonality model was used to forecast tanker demand.

findings.title: West Hyderabad is a real hotspot
findings.text: Areas like KPHB, Nizampet, Kondapur, and Gachibowli form a statistically significant high-stress cluster (Moran's I = 0.313, p = 0.001), driven mainly by tanker dependency. The interactive map shows all 185 water-supply sections, colored on a gradient by their water stress score — sections with higher scores sit at the stressed end of the color scale, so the West Hyderabad cluster stands out at a glance.

findings.title: Rainfall is not the cause
findings.text: Rainfall from 1901 to 2021 shows a slight increase, not a decline, so the stress looks more like demand growth outpacing infrastructure in fast-growing areas. This chart plots annual rainfall with a trend line, showing a slight rise over the century with large year-to-year swings, which is why rainfall is ruled out as the main driver.

findings.title: Tanker demand is rising
findings.text: Citywide bookings grew by about 1,149 per month, with a clear peak from April to June (R² = 0.93). The chart shows monthly tanker bookings from 2022 to early 2024, with the fitted trend and a projection into mid-2024. With only about two years of data behind it, the projection shows direction rather than exact numbers.

title: Women's Empowerment Archetypes in India
description: Three empowerment archetypes identified from NFHS-5 survey data on 60,480 women using PCA and K-Means, mapped at state and district level.
downloadNote: Individual-level download restricted — NFHS-5 microdata terms do not allow redistribution. Aggregated results are shown on the map above; for the underlying data, register directly with the DHS Program (source link below).
introText: Empowerment is usually reduced to a single score. This project asks whether Indian women fall into distinct types instead. Using NFHS-5 survey data for 60,480 women, it groups women by economic participation and say in household decisions, then maps how household autonomy varies across states and districts.
methodology:
The survey file has over 700,000 respondents and 500+ columns, so the work began by selecting 12 relevant variables and checking each against the dataset's own codebook. That check caught a wrong variable code before it caused problems. Most of the data appeared blank at first, and the cause turned out to be the survey design rather than errors:
- The employment and finance questions were only asked of a random 15% of women, so the analysis was limited to that group and their matching survey weight was used.
- One question was skipped for women with no earnings. Instead of dropping those women, "no personal earnings" was kept as its own category.

Decision-making answers were converted into a 0 to 2 autonomy scale. PCA showed that empowerment has several independent dimensions, and K-Means clustering (with the number of groups chosen by silhouette score) produced three archetypes. Results were then mapped at state, urban/rural, and district level. This included matching 707 districts to a boundary file, fixing duplicate district names (seven names repeat across states), renamed districts, and post-2011 splits.

A visual check of the map then exposed a flaw in the method. Archetype percentages always sum to 100%, so a state with low employment automatically shows a larger "homemaker" share. Archetypes are therefore reported only as a national result, and a separate continuous autonomy score is used for the geographic comparison.

findings.title: Three archetypes describe Indian women's empowerment
findings.text: Weighted to the national level, 59.0% are 'Homemaker with Household Voice' (not working, but with real say in household decisions), 25.3% are 'Economically Active & Autonomous', and 15.7% are 'Fully Constrained'. The Fully Constrained figure is probably a floor rather than a ceiling, since the survey requires a private interview, and the most controlling households are less likely to allow one.

findings.title: Education and age at marriage barely separate the groups
findings.text: Average education and age at marriage were nearly identical across all three archetypes. What separates them is economic participation and decision-making power — two different dimensions rather than one scale.

findings.title: Geography does not follow the usual assumptions
findings.text: Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana had some of the highest Fully Constrained shares (20 to 22%), while Nagaland and Mizoram had the lowest. In several states, including Telangana, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu, rural women were more economically active than urban women. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh scored at or above several southern states on the autonomy score, and only Tamil Nadu and Kerala clearly ranked higher. The interactive map colors each district by its household autonomy score using rank-based bins, since the actual scores span a narrow range (0.65 to 1.19). About 3% of districts could not be matched to the boundary file and appear grey.

limitations: The measure covers only self-reported say over a few household decisions, not overall development, and "joint" decisions can mean either real partnership or token consultation. Small states like Ladakh and Chandigarh have few respondents, so their numbers are less reliable.

title: Hyderabad Metro Expansion
description: Scores every 1 km square of Hyderabad by transit need and proposes 3 new metro corridors that would bring the most underserved people within walking distance per km of line.
introText: Which parts of Hyderabad have the most people living far from a metro station, and where would new lines reach the most of them? This project combines open map and population data into a 1 km grid of the city and scores how much each square needs the metro, then proposes the 3 new corridors that would bring the most unserved people within walking distance per kilometre of line, routed along wide roads.
methodology:
OpenStreetMap (metro stations, bus stops, schools, colleges and roads) and WorldPop population data were combined for 693 one-kilometre squares covering about 7.8 million people. Most of the effort went into the data and the scoring:
- The city was defined from population data, because the official boundary had holes and left out parts of Secunderabad.
- Patchy OpenStreetMap coverage of bus stops and schools was handled by widening the search, and the score is treated as relative need.
- Six planned and under-construction Old City stations were removed, so only the 64 operational stations count as "served".
- Hand-picked job hubs stand in for commuting, because real commute data isn't openly available.

The need score is demand (people 50%, schools 25%, colleges 25%) multiplied by gap (distance to the metro 60%, job hubs 30%, bus stops 10%). A simple average pushed the top scores to the empty edges of the city, so the two halves are multiplied instead: a square needs both many people and poor access to rank high.

The highest-need squares were grouped into 12 hotspots. Candidate lines were routed along trunk, primary and secondary roads. They may only start at the end of an existing line or at a junction (7 allowed start points), can't exceed 15 km, and can't be more than 1.8 times longer than a straight line. Each route is scored by the unserved people within 1 km of it, divided by its length. Stations were placed about every 1.25 km, counting the people within an 800 m walk.

findings.title: Three new lines would bring about 441,000 people within walking distance of a station
findings.text: Line 1 starts at LB Nagar (South), runs 5.9 km with 5 stations, reaching 83,330 people. Line 2 starts at JBS Parade Ground (North), runs 10.3 km with 8 stations, reaching 191,874 people. Line 3 starts at Miyapur (West), runs 10.3 km with 8 stations, reaching 165,766 people. The map above shows existing lines in their own colours, with each proposed line in a darker shade of the line it extends.

findings.title: The three winning hotspots are not the highest-scoring ones
findings.text: Ranked by average need score, the hotspots behind Lines 3, 1 and 2 come 9th, 10th and 11th out of 12. A high need score marks a place that is underserved, but a good corridor also has to be reachable from an allowed start point, stay within the length limit, and reach many unserved people for each kilometre built.

findings.title: The biggest hotspot misses out by a narrow margin
findings.text: The south-west of the city (roughly Mehdipatnam, Tolichowki and Attapur) is the largest hotspot, with about 368,000 people and the second-highest need score — but it wasn't chosen. Only one allowed start point (MG Bus Station) could reach it within the 15 km limit, and even that 8.8 km route reaches about 17,203 people per km, roughly 10% below Line 3 and well below Line 1's 25,596. About half the people along that route already live within 1.5 km of an existing station, so they don't count as unserved.

findings.title: The hotspot pattern holds up when the scoring weights change
findings.text: Between 92% and 94% of the hotspot squares stayed the same when the metro, bus, and job-hub weights were changed — the three winning corridors aren't an artifact of one particular weighting choice.

limitations: OpenStreetMap is missing some bus stops, schools, and colleges, so the need score is relative, not absolute. Distance to job hubs stands in for real commuting data, which isn't openly available. Population is a WorldPop model estimate, not a census count. The 15 km length limit and the extension-or-junction start rule decide which hotspots can be reached at all — a wide road doesn't guarantee a metro can actually be built there. These are priority corridors for further study, not a final alignment.
